# Solution

**Claim:** The cardinality of the set of all equivalence relations on $\mathbb{N}$ with all equivalence classes of the same cardinality is $2^{\aleph_0}$.

## Upper Bound

An equivalence relation on $\mathbb{N}$ is a subset of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$. Since $|\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}| = \aleph_0$, the power set $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N})$ has cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$. The set of equivalence relations (with the equal-cardinality condition or not) is a subset of this power set, so its cardinality is at most $2^{\aleph_0}$.

## Lower Bound

It suffices to exhibit a subfamily of size $2^{\aleph_0}$. Consider equivalence relations where every class has exactly **2** elements (perfect matchings of $\mathbb{N}$).

**Construction of an injection $2^{\mathbb{N}} \hookrightarrow \{\text{perfect matchings of } \mathbb{N}\}$:**

Partition $\mathbb{N}$ into consecutive blocks of four:
$$B_k = \{4k,\; 4k+1,\; 4k+2,\; 4k+3\}, \quad k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$$

For each subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, define a perfect matching $M_A$ by specifying the pairing within each block $B_k$:

- If $k \in A$: pair $(4k, 4k{+}1)$ and $(4k{+}2, 4k{+}3)$.
- If $k \notin A$: pair $(4k, 4k{+}2)$ and $(4k{+}1, 4k{+}3)$.

**$M_A$ is a perfect matching:** Every element of $\mathbb{N}$ belongs to exactly one block $B_k$, and within each block every element is paired with exactly one other. So $M_A$ partitions $\mathbb{N}$ into 2-element classes.

**The map $A \mapsto M_A$ is injective:** If $A \neq A'$, there exists $k$ belonging to one but not the other. Within block $B_k$, the pairings differ (one uses $\{4k,4k{+}1\}$, the other uses $\{4k,4k{+}2\}$), so $M_A \neq M_{A'}$.

This gives an injection from $2^{\mathbb{N}}$ (cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$) into the set of equivalence relations on $\mathbb{N}$ where all classes have cardinality 2. Each such equivalence relation satisfies the "all classes have the same cardinality" condition.

## Conclusion

- **Upper bound:** $\leq 2^{\aleph_0}$ (subset of $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N})$).
- **Lower bound:** $\geq 2^{\aleph_0}$ (injection from $2^{\mathbb{N}}$ via perfect matchings with class size 2).

By the Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein theorem, the cardinality is exactly

$$\boxed{2^{\aleph_0}}.$$
